utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. No preliminaries. Therefore, we briefly go into closed session in order to allow the witness to enter the courtroom, and after that we'll return into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Witness RM279, before we resume, I'd like to remind you that you're still -- there apparently is a problem with the audio. Can you hear me now -- or can you hear the interpreter, rather? Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you hear me now? You can hear the interpreter now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness RM279, before we resume, I'd like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony; that is, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, one question that came to me before I get back to the questions we left off at last session. I want to ask you about something that some of the documents show, especially the documents of intercepts from the police entity. They say that the "Pale radio relay" was being monitored. Do you have knowledge of what communications node of the former JNA this would be in reference to?

utterances.speaker: RM279 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I do know is that the task assigned to the personnel of the State Security Service was to monitor the so-called political communication. The political leadership of Republika Srpska was in Pale. Pale is located similarly to Zvornik. It was probably the end point radio relay station, which most likely went via Jahorina and to Veliki Zep. That way, they could monitor the frequency arriving from Veliki Zep going on to Pale and the other way around, and they were able to listen in.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that. And now I'd like to take off where we left off yesterday at document 1D1067 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But if we could please not broadcast that to the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And this is in relation to the testimony that we just started about you having received money from the Office of the Prosecution of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could you just give the ID number again, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 2 in both versions of this document. And now we have it up on the screen in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: As you can see, sir, this is a note to file by an attorney of the Prosecution team dated 21 May, 2010, but reporting of something that occurred in May of 2007. And I will not be mentioning your name, but it says here that you were retained by the OTP in May 2007 as a consultant --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, there is a problem with the translation. I'm told the B/C/S translation is not coming through to either co-counsel or to the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand from Mr. Stojanovic's gestures that it has been fixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I will start from the beginning. This document talks about something that occurred in May of 2007, and it says you were retained by the OTP in May of 2007 as a consultant to evaluate the expert report entitled: "Analysis of Interception of Radio Relay Communication of the Army of Republika Srpska," dated 23 April, 2007, and the evidence of Popovic Defence expert, Djuro Rodic, concerning the interception capabilities of the ABiH 2nd Corps Anti-Electronic Warfare Unit. It says you rendered consultative services to the OTP from 16 May to 25 May 2007 for which you received remuneration in the amount of 2.000 US dollars, travel expenses, and the applicable daily subsistence allowance. Sir, is the information contained in this letter truthful and accurate that you were a consultant for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: RM279 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, is the information contained in this letter truthful and accurate that you were paid 2.000 US dollars, plus travel expenses, plus daily subsistence expenses?

utterances.speaker: RM279 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know precisely. I said in my testimony that I received around 1 and a half thousand German marks. They paid for my hotel and expenses from here. I can't recall the figure exactly, but it certainly wasn't more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now if you look at the end of the letter on the bottom of the page in both languages, it says you: "Conceded that often there were imbalances in the audibility of collocutors in intercepted conversations and that sometimes only one speaker could be heard. He explained that this phenomena in terms of duplex 2 frequencies and simplex single frequency radio transmissions but noted that the VRS's poor equipment and maintenance practices, as well as the failure of its personnel to follow basic protective protocols contributed to the ability of the anti-electronic warfare unit to intercept duplex communications on a single frequency." Sir, is this letter truthful and accurate as to this recitation of what it was that you told the Office of the Prosecutor back in May of 2007?

utterances.speaker: RM279 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is absolutely correct. The question was how can one sometimes hear both interlocutors, whereas on other occasions one could only hear one on the same frequency. We were taught in school that were two basic reasons for it. One of the reasons is feedback, because the microphone and the headset have basically the same function. If the operator speaks loudly enough, it is picked up by his own head phone and that can be heard in communication. There can also be differences in workstation at radio relay nodes which can be switched and that is why some communication can be picked up in that fashion although not always.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document as the next exhibit number under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1067 receives number D135, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if you could tell us, sir, in relation to both the average monthly salary in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 2007 in terms of your pension, how did the 2.000 US dollars plus expenses compare, or how would it compare to both of those?

utterances.speaker: RM279 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you're really interested it's around two of my monthly pensions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: For the next two questions I'd like to go into private session to protect the identity of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the record show that the last 65 ter number is actually 316 not 136.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours it's D316.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we can now call up number 04712 but not broadcast the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, what we have here is a document that indicates a joint commission was composed by both ICTY and BH personnel to make a selection of documents to be used as evidence. And looking at this document, can it -- it identifies that you participated in this. Can you confirm that, in fact, you participated in this event when 148 documents were selected for evidence in April of 1998 by a joint commission that included OTP staff?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, where can I find any reference to a joint commission in this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Line 2 in the English, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am familiar with this record. I

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't know if we need to have any --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you tell us what criteria was used to select documents for use as evidence?

utterances.speaker: RM279 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, there was no criteria. Whatever notebooks we had at the time were piled together, a list was created, and they were handed over.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I want to ask you if you considered your work in selecting documents was intended to assist the Prosecution to obtain convictions of former VRS officers?

utterances.speaker: RM279 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see it that I way. I did my job, I did what I was ordered to do. There was no particular selection of documents. Only in the first case did we make a selection singling out the documents pertaining to General Krstic. The rest of it went in bulk.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You said, sir, that you did what you were ordered to. Did you have orders from your superiors to the effect that you should select documents to assist the Prosecution to obtain convictions of former VRS officers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you clearly explain, because otherwise the witness who is not a lawyer, Mr. Ivetic, in normal language for someone not being a lawyer what you are seeking from the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me try and make it as simple as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were you ordered to give everything to the Prosecution or were you ordered to give only a selection of items to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a different question. That's a different question. Let me see. I gave you an opportunity to rephrase, but if you -- What Mr. Ivetic would like to know is whether by providing this material, whether selection or all of it, whether it was your purpose to have persons to be convicted - that is, to be punished for what they had done wrong - whether that was your intention when providing this? Is this what was on your mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're absolutely right, Mr. President. I had no agenda, no intention. Either myself or anyone else. Everyone is innocent until proven guilty. It seems that already during the hand-over some people believed that people would be convicted, but I did it in military terms. I handed over the document without paying any regard to the fact whether someone would be convicted or not. We had no contact with them. We simply went about our work which at some points became relevant in terms of the documents relating to some events in Bosnia and Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to tender this document under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 04712 receives number D317, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we can have another document, 1D1068, and also not broadcast this one to the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, what we have on the screen is a Tribunal witness statement prepared by the Office of the Prosecutor and it's for an individual whose name I will not mention, but I ask you to look at that name and tell us if it is someone you are familiar with and in fact someone who was a member of the same unit?

utterances.speaker: RM279 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, looking at this information, I can say that the name is familiar. I believe that he was here, too. Year of birth. This is an engineer of safety and protection at work as far as I remember, and he was a commander of a squad in facilities in the north.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, if we look at the persons listed as present for the interview, we see the names of various Prosecution personnel, and then we see your name as well. Can you confirm that you were present at this interview and at the time that this statement was taken from this individual?

utterances.speaker: RM279 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it says here, I believe it's true, but I cannot really remember at this moment because I spoke to many people. I can't even see the date, really. Oh, yes, there it is. Yeah, probably. I know all these people from the OTP, so probably I was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can I ask you, sir, how many other interviews of potential witnesses with the Office of the Prosecutor did you participate in?

utterances.speaker: RM279 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't recall. Whatever -- however hard I try, I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would it be more than one?

utterances.speaker: RM279 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall why it was that you were present and what your role was at the interview -- in this Prosecution interview and in this Prosecution witness statement?

utterances.speaker: RM279 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that my role here was only that of an electronic warfare officer, to be present as a host.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The statement or are you just -- I don't know whether it's just a cover page, because that's apparently the presence of the witness is what seems to --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Be the problem, right. What I would then do is then I would ask that it be MFI'd so that we can mange sure. I think that the version I have is just the cover page but I notice in e-court there is more pages, so I just need to -- I just need the cover sheet just to memorialise the name of the other person so I can make sure that that is corrected in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then what we have in front of us is a five-page document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are interested in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Cover sheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- cover sheet. It will be MFI'd. And you can upload the cover sheet only.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1 068 receives number D318, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification under seal. I add to this that D316 we discussed earlier, which was also MFI'd, is also MFI'd under seal. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now one last document I would look at with you, sir. It's 65 ter number 04713.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And again, we should not broadcast the same to be safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And this is -- oh, I should wait for the English. Sir, this is another correspondence evidencing the hand-over materials from the BiH side to the -- to the Prosecutor, dated April of 1998 in relation to the intercepts and notebooks, and it says here that it is being given to an ICTY representative, but you'll see here that there is no title or ICTY title for the person taking these materials but rather he appears to be an active member of the United States army at the time of the hand-over. Can you recall or explain for us why it is that the materials would have been handed over to a member of the United States army?

utterances.speaker: RM279 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot explain why this was handed to a member of the US army, but he was a member of that group so we didn't ask any questions. We just asked for their IDs so that we could draft this record. I remember the gentleman. He went to the facilities, he listened to the communications, but whether he as a US army member worked for ICTY, I don't know. We were ordered to put the tapes into boxes, close them, glue them closed, and marked them. He received them and took them away.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, if this gentleman for the US army who was given this material was, in fact, an intelligence officer of the US army or do you know what branch he was from?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Lee.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think the witness just testified that he did not know whether -- whether he was an active member of the US army. He believed that it was a member of the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now --

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: So I think this [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Lee, Ms. Lee, Mr. Ivetic is entitled to put some follow-up questions to further, perhaps a bit more profoundly, deal with the matter. So could the witness please answer, if he is able to do so, the question that was put.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, on the occasion of the hand-over of these tapes, I was simply ordered to pack them, make a list of them, and hand them over. The standard procedure was when I typed this record with the gentleman to ask him to produce his ID. He gave me that card and I simply copied information from it. I didn't think about him being a member of the army or not. He was in civilian clothes, so I never really gave it a thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would tender this document under seal as the next exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 04713 receives number D319, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Witness, I thank you for answering my questions. I have nothing further for you today.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We briefly move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Ms. Lee will now have some further questions for you in re-examination. Ms. Lee, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. May I please have 65 ter number -- excuse me, Exhibit 1622.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's under seal and should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Witness, during cross-examination you were asked a question relating to this specific intercept and you were asked to provide an explanation as to why the identity of General Krstic was revealed but that in parenthesis it was written "could not be heard." Do you recall that part of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: RM279 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] At that time your answer was: "I don't know. You would have to ask the gentleman who wrote this conversation." And if I were to tell you that in an interview with the Office of the Prosecutor, the intercept operator who wrote this conversation was asked about this specific intercept.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And now may I please have 65 ter number 29028, not to be broadcast to public because it is under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: May I please have 1D01070, and if I could have that not to be broadcast to the public.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you recognise the name of this individual?

utterances.speaker: RM279 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is there no B/C/S translation?

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: I don't -- this is a -- I don't believe a B/C/S translation has been uploaded. This is a Defence document that I'm just referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And if this individual said that Mr. Krstic usually gave his name, and not only do we know his voice, we knew many of the voices of the officers as well. And I'd like to show you --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is there a question or are we going to have the counsel giving commentary and giving evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm getting to my question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And I would like to know were there several other individuals that have -- that were -- I'll strike that. Now -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Lee, would it assist you if we take a break?

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. If we could take a break at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was already time for the break, so that is the main reason. We briefly turn into closed session so as to allow the witness to leave the courtroom. We'll resume in 20 minutes from now, again in closed session, then to return in open session immediately after that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Ms. Lee, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Witness, in your 92 ter statement, and this is P1614, you

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: May we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Witness, did the VRS known that their communications were being heard by the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: RM279 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only say so based on the conversations we heard. They didn't know that we were listening in for only a year, but they knew it for three years, and often operators and different people mentioned that radio traffic procedures should be followed as well as protection procedures. However, it all depended on the person's position.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: May I please have 65 ter number 20996AA, and it should be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Lee, I'm informed that an English translation is missing. I see there is communication without words between Madam Registrar and the team manager of the OTP. The OTP indicating that it's uploaded, Madam Registrar trying to establish whether it has been received.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: In the -- in the meantime, we could call up another document if that assists. No?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It should be there in a second, I take it. It's all about communications. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now it's there.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And in this document it says: "X: Krstic has just come up here. He went back there, he'll call me later. He'll look into it and will assign someone to co-ordinate it ... yes, yes, I know ... hey listen, I know. Just take it easy, this is an open line." Witness, do you -- do you recognise this document to be one that would have been produced by your unit?

utterances.speaker: RM279 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is probably from my unit. Without the cover page of the notebook I can't say anything precisely, but it is probably from our unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And in this intercept it mentions an open line. Was this an indication for you to know whether or not the VRS knew that you are intercepting their -- that the ARBiH was intercepting their conversation?

utterances.speaker: RM279 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll repeat yet again. The Army of Republika Srpska knew 100 per cent that we were monitoring such conversations. But might makes right. They were the stronger one and they behaved the way they did. In terms of the lie of the land, and hopefully I'm saying this for the last time: In military terms, we had ideal monitoring facilities. In any situation, in any terrain, and with any party, probably one will never have another opportunity like that. These facilities were part of the communications system of the JNA before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And -- thank you. You've testified today that the VRS personnel did not always follow protocol. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: RM279 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: May I please have P -- [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: This phone was ringing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Someone was calling, no one picks up the phone. That's okay. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Actually, before we move on, can I -- may I please tender 20996AA into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 20996AA receives number P1639, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Under seal?

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see whether we need it under seal. Could you give it some more thought, Ms. Lee, soon, whether it really needs to be under seal as being just one page, one isolated page of the document?

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: It has -- it contains a signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It contains a signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Of an intercept operator, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Under seal. Mr. Ivetic, could I inquire with you. Is there any dispute about awareness of the VRS that possibly they were monitored? So I'm not asking anything about whether it could be done but whether there was concern about being monitored, an awareness of -- well, that this could happen?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No dispute, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No dispute. Ms. Lee, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: May I please have P1305 [Realtime transcript read in error "P105"] onto the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's supposed to be 1305, P1305. P1305.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And it should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Lee, we have it on our screens now.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Witness, is this a document -- is this a document that would have come from your unit?

utterances.speaker: RM279 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The left-hand side document in Bosnian does originate from the northern facility. On the right-hand side, the translation is not identical to the original.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is -- I will only be referring to the conversation contained in -- at conversation 11:49, and that's the only conversation I will be relying on, and so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you then seek the corresponding B/C/S version, what page is that in e-court?

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: It's e-court page 2, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Page 2, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, it is on the second page that we find the corresponding B/C/S. There we are. I think we have established this earlier. You'll find it at the bottom of the page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Witness, this is an intercept from 11:49, and it says participants panorama 3, switchboard, and Lieutenant-Colonel Savcic. Do you see that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RM279 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And then when you read towards the beginning, it starts: "C: Who wants to know? "P: Panorama 3. "C: Panorama B? "P: Panorama 3. "C: Ah-ha, you need Lieutenant-Colonel Savcic, right? "P: Go fuck yourself, you stupid idiot. "C: Just a moment, you're connected." And further down, if we could go to the next page -- oh, on B/C/S, yes, that's on it, it says: "Slow down --"

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Can we go down in the English version as well. Can we go to the next page on the English version? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: It says: "P: Slow down. Slow down. Don't talk too much. You should know better. And tell that idiot there next time not to mention any names, ranks, or last names. "S: Who is this? "P: We know each other well, you and I. "S: And whom should I ask ... "P: Panorama, man, don't do this, you're worse than the man before you!" Now based on this -- on -- on what you see on this intercept, does this confirm that the VRS personnel did not follow the basic protocols when transmitting communications?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would object to the [indiscernible] conclusion that it goes beyond the document that is before us.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm asking whether -- or reading by -- by reading this intercept it confirms what he had testified to today in D315.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what you want to know from the witness is whether he recognises this as an example of what he said --

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Said before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- before that procedures were not --

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Followed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- followed. Do you recognise this as an example of not following procedures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next question please, Ms. Lee.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: May I please have 65 ter number 29041 on e-court, please. And my I've the usher's assistance to provide this notebook to the witness. I would like to have the first page, the picture page on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, is it -- could I ask whether it's the Defence's position that the Snow White and the Seven Dwarves originate from 2012 or that it may have been produced earlier? 2001, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's our position, sir, that we don't know when this book was produced, and there is a -- as I believe I was very precise in my wording that there was a stamp on the beginning of the cover page from the manufacturer that had this notation. And we don't know what it means at this point. But we do not believe that the book originally from 1995, that it was from sometime subsequent from 1995, and we're still undertaking investigations to determine that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do we have the original somewhere so that we can see whether it's the stamp or --

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: The original has been provided to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we have for one second a look at it? Do the parties agree, you talked about a stamp, Mr. Ivetic, that's the reason why the Chamber wanted to look at it, but it is a part of the print that resembles a stamp but is just part of the print of the cover.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: From the manufacturer which is what I said when I asked the witness this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, just a minute ago you talked about a stamp. And, Ms. Lee, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Witness, have you examined the document before you, the book before -- notebook before you, and does it correspond to the image that you have in front of the screen?

utterances.speaker: RM279 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: In the bottom left corner there is a place where you have presumably an image which corresponds to a finger-print of this chipmunk that's appearing on the image. I just want to -- for you to see whether or not the picture form is part of a cover rather than any stamp that may have placed by anyone else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be no dispute about that, that it's not a stamp placed by anyone else than the entity which produced the cover.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Lee.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Yes, and I just wanted to clarify for the record that there is no manufacturing stamp but it's just part of a cover that's part of the image, the graphic, that's appearing as -- on the notebook. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but it's agreed upon by the parties so we can continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Then may I please have this exhibit entered into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 29041 receives number P1640, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Public?

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Public exhibit, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, before I give you an opportunity to further examine the witness, I would have one question for you, Witness, which is the following: You testified about your presence during interviews, and you said your role was being a host. Now what came to my mind, and please either confirm or deny that that would have been part of your role, is that if you're interviewing someone on a very technical matter such as the communications that having someone, a consultant, available who could assist in phrasing questions and could assist in understanding answers given on these technical nature, that seemed to me a role you may well have played. Was that part of your role as well apart from being a host?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Mr. President. You put it well. One of the reasons was that. The other reason was that the documents pertained to the period when I was in command. By sheer circumstance, the person who was my predecessor went to another commanding duty and I replaced him. So it was by sheer coincidence that I happened to be there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic, any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just briefly. And I'll start with the ones in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked at length by the Prosecutor about this intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can call up on the screen P1622, and that broadcast -- should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you were asked about the possibility that the intercept operator may have heard the switchboard and then jotted it down from that even though the person identified as General Krstic could not be heard. We just looked at an intercept where there was a switchboard involved and the words of the switchboard were identified in the conversation and there was in the introduction or header the switchboard was also identified. Can you confirm for me, sir, that in the handwritten portion of this original B/C/S from this operator from one of the stations, there is no mention of a switchboard identifying one of the participants as Krstic?

utterances.speaker: RM279 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. There is no mention but probably they heard it during the conversation and only once they heard it they started making notes of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can call up P169 under seal and so it should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If you recall your direct examination from the other day, this particular conversation was actually the subject of an intercept by the other unit, the other station of your unit, and the document that we're about to look at is the handwritten notebook from that intercept operator.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: P1619, I apologise, under seal. It should not be broadcast. If it helps, it's 65 ter number 21135B, as in Beta.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we look in the B/C/S, it's at the top of the page, and in the English it's the only part of the document that's been translated, can we confirm that in this second intercept operator intercepting this very same communication there again is no reference to any switchboard operator having identified the participants?

utterances.speaker: RM279 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is written in the notebook is really like that, but this was done in the north and you see that this is about a general. And these things are noted in context. You listen and you hear what -- who calls and who replies. I, of course, cannot give any definitive explanation. You'd have to ask the one who wrote this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Agreed. And I think I don't need to go through this with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But, Your Honours, also we have P1621 which was the police intercept related to this conversation that also has no reference to a switchboard, although it was taken from the 2nd Army Dispatch. So I don't believe that they had a separate intercept, it's just relaying what this -- what their information was from these intercepts. I'd like to now go into private session to deal with one other matter that arose during cross-examination -- during redirect examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, I have only a general question about all the notebooks we have seen, the original and the copies in e-court. Where did you get these notebooks from? They are -- they don't look like a typical military -- yeah, booklet, but it was obviously produced for another purpose. Where did you get that from and when? How did you obtain these booklets?

utterances.speaker: RM279 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know the source, but in early 1995 the market in Bosnia was more open so there were more things to buy than before. We had no official printed documents in our units because those were expensive and resource intensive. We got some notebooks from logistics. We had always applied for them. And I remember that we exchanged some notebooks for flour in the headquarters building. But up until summer 1995, we used anything to write on. We used flimsy paper and held it together with paper clips, for example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have an observation but not necessarily a question. There seems to be dispute between the parties whether the notebooks were manufactured before July 1995. I do understand that the Defence takes the position that they have been produced after 1995, and that it is the position of the Prosecution that they were produced before July 1995. Is that -- does that reflect your positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With respect to some of the notebooks, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It's our position that 1 Gennaio 2001 is the date that Popotia was assigned her identity card from this child's notebook, and so, yes, that's the dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's the dispute. I noticed that on the left part of the cover of this notebook there is a bar code. Now, very often bar codes provide a lot of information about producer, manufacturer, and sometimes even more; that is, what batch it was, et cetera. Has it been explored what the bar code tell us?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We -- we did this in the Popovic case and came to a dead-end. Couldn't resolve the issue and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then just for my information that it's hereby on the record that that doesn't lead us to any resolution whether the one way or the other way. Then there are no further questions for the witness. This then concludes, Witness, your testimony. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again. We turn into closed session in order to allow the witness to leave the courtroom. We'll then take immediately the break so as to prepare for the voice distortion of the next witness. And then we'll resume in closed session, again. And then once the witness is in, we turn into open or private session. One second, please. One second.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Witness RM316, before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness RM316, you will give your testimony with protective measures; that is, face distortion, no one will see your face outside this courtroom; voice distortion, no one will hear your own voice outside this courtroom; and pseudonym, we do not use your own name. We'll call you "Witness" or "Witness RM316." You'll first be examined by Mr. Jeremy. You'll find him to your right. Mr. Jeremy is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: RM316
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness kindly be asked to approach the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you come a bit closer to the microphone, Witness. Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Witness, you've been informed about the protective measures in place for you. In addition to these, if you feel an answer might reveal your identity or relate to a private matter, then feel free to ask the Judges to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: RM316
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see on our screens 65 ter 29002, which should not be broadcast. It is a pseudonym sheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, without reading aloud what is on the screen, can you see your name?

utterances.speaker: RM316
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And at the bottom of the screen [microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And at the bottom of the screen, is that your correct date of birth?

utterances.speaker: RM316
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender into evidence 65 ter 29002, under seal as the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 29002 receives number P1653, Your Honours, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1653 is admitted into evidence under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, did you testify in the case of Prosecutor versus Tolimir on the 27th of May, 2010?

utterances.speaker: RM316
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And did you listen to a recording of your evidence in that case in preparation for your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: RM316
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And did this recording accurately reflect what you said in the Tolimir case?

utterances.speaker: RM316
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And do you affirm the truthfulness and accuracy of that testimony?

utterances.speaker: RM316
utterances.text: Yes, I affirm that everything I said is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And lastly, if you are asked the same questions today during those proceedings -- during these proceedings, sorry, as you were asked in that case, would you give the same answers in substance?

utterances.speaker: RM316
utterances.text: Yes. I believe I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution tenders, under seal, 65 ter 29001 as the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just want to draw your attention to the fact, and we also discussed it recently since we were not actually aware of it, the witnesses were asked to confirm audio, and then transcript was introduced. And we saw on many occasions that there were discrepancies. So I think that should be cured somehow. If -- this witness cannot confirm that the transcript is accurate. He confirmed that audio is transcript -- accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, if there are any concerns about discrepancies between audio and transcript in relation to this witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We don't have audio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't have audio but --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think maybe we do [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I think you have certainly access to audio.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think Ms. Stewart is nodding that we do. But I didn't check audio, I was reading only transcript. And I told you only a couple of days ago we actually were concerned about this issue. We were not thinking about it before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a valid issue you're raising, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I understand that the B/C/S audio for all of the witnesses we are calling has been disclosed to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the Chamber, of course, is aware that usually the transcript is fairly accurate, and if there's -- if it's noticed at any moment that mistakes are made, and mistakes, of course, are human, then they will be corrected immediately. Now, if there is anything which remained unnoticed, a discrepancy between audio and transcript, then, of course, the Chamber is quite willing to consider that. And most important, if you would inform the Prosecution about it, I take it that they'll draw the attention of the witness to that. But we, of course, we can't start comparing the original. That's a bit of a problem because it is, first of all, the audio in B/C/S; second, it is then the transcript on the basis of the translation by the interpreters, the interpretation. If there is any concern at any moment or if there is any vital matter where you would like to raise this matter, of course, the Chamber is open to hear it. If it is your position that we should not, for that reason, further admit into evidence the transcripts, then it needs a bit more than just a loose observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, first it's not our job to check their 65 ter statements -- 92 ter statements. It's their job. We will not be asking them to check if our -- if we introduce some transcripts. We don't have manpower to check audio and transcripts. We cannot do that. They are much more powerful. So if they want to introduce transcripts, they should make certain that transcript is accurate transcription of audio. So it cannot be continued this way, that they check audio and then introduce transcripts. And it's not our job to check it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the general rule in this Tribunal is that the parties and the Bench rely on the accuracy of interpretation and transcription up till the moment where there are reasons to believe that mistakes are made, identified by whomever. I think that is done all the time. The Chamber relies on the interpretation and the transcript when we are preparing for the judgements, for example, when we are evaluating the evidence, and to require that a party should do that job again is not something that comes to my mind at this moment. But, again, I said if you want to do more than just to raise the issue in this case and without any specific complaints but more in general, then you would have to make more thorough submissions on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we will consider them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just again if I may, this is 92 ter statement. The witness is, according to the Rules, required to confirm the accuracy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I do understand that that is your position, but if you want to change in a rather dramatic way the practice which was applied in many cases, and was applied in this case consistently, which you are fully entitled to do, then we cannot do it in five minutes with oral arguments, then you should make thorough written submissions on the matter, the Defence will have opportunity to respond to that, and then the Chamber will consider it. Of course, the Prosecution will further respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not to discourage you to do it, but if you do it then you should do it thoroughly. Does that mean at this moment that you object against admission?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we do object against the admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jeremy, any response to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: The particular transcript that we're relying on is from the Tolimir case. I understand that the transcript was checked carefully as that case went through, and any corrections that needed to be made were made at the time. It's the -- it's been the practice with all 92 ter witnesses who testified in B/C/S for whom we only have a English transcript that they listen to the audio of the B/C/S and confirm the accuracy of that audio, and on the basis of that we rely on the CLSS translations and we rely on the accuracy of the transcripts from each of the cases that we rely and to tender via 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I may -- one thing before you start, Your Honours, please. The previous witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may add something, Mr. Lukic, although -- let me see, yes. Yes. You are. You --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The previous witness corrected his transcript also from Tolimir case on multiple occasions, today and days before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any other objections, Mr. Lukic, apart from the one you raised?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll see at the end if there are some discrepancies or not. I cannot tell you now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And that's the only objection what we can raise at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If it turns out that there are discrepancies, of course the Chamber will further consider those discrepancies. The Chamber denies the objection and will follow the practice it has followed in this case. But, as I said before, we certainly do not discourage you to raise the issue in thorough submissions, we'll then receive the responses, and whether that will then change anything, we'll see that. At this moment, Madam Registrar, the transcript would receive number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 29001 receives number P1654, Your Honours, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1654 is admitted into evidence under seal. Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, as regards associated exhibits, I anticipate using some of these during the course of the direct examination. Although there are only four that I'm not -- already admitted into evidence, but I would propose to deal with them at the end, at the conclusion of the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you would prepare a list later whether the descriptions are -- that Madam Registrar can already prepare the assignment of numbers to it and we'll deal with it at the end of the testimony of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would now like to read a short summary of this witness's evidence, the purpose of which I have explained to the witness. During 1994 and 1995, the witness was an employee of the State Security Service or SDB and was involved in the monitoring, recording, and transcribing of intercepted radio signal communications involving the VRS and the Bosnian Serb leadership. He describes the location at which this was conducted, the staff involved, the equipment used, and all stages of the process and procedures involved in the intercepting and transcribing of those intercepted communications. This witness was personally involved in all aspects of this process. In particular, the witness describes how the team would intercept VRS communications. If an intercept operator considered an intercepted conversation important, this would be recorded using a reel-to-reel recorder known as a UHER, U-H-E-R, once recorded, while the first man continued to monitor the radio waves, typically, a second would transcribe the recorded conversation onto paper. It would then be typed from the paper into a computer, encrypted, manually logged in an index, and sent to the headquarters. The witness also details the meticulous steps taken to ensure that intercepted communications were accurately recorded and speakers within those conversations accurately identified. That concludes the summary, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jeremy. If you have any further questions, you may put them to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Witness, in your Tolimir testimony, Exhibit P1654, you provide a brief overview of the interception process in which your unit was engaged. And I'd like to fill in some of the details of that. You say that you had a four-man team who worked in shifts of two. That's from transcript page 2054, e-court page 9. You also state your team operated from a northern location, as did the 2nd Corps of the ABiH. My question is: Did your team work in the same room as the ABiH or was it a different room?

utterances.speaker: RM316
utterances.text: We were in the same facility, the facility being one of the former armed forces where all of the premises were used by the 2nd PEB 2nd Corps. One of such rooms was assigned to us. In the room, we set up work, and that is where the entire process took place. That is also where the people rested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could I already now ask you to focus your answers on what was asked. The question simply was: Were you in the same room with the ABiH. The answer simply was no, you were not in the same room. And whether someone was resting there or whether -- that's all, whether it was set up for work. If Mr. Jeremy would like to know, he'll certainly ask you. Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Witness, in your written evidence, P1654, you provide an overview of the equipment you used in the interception process. And I'm not going to ask you to do that again. But what I would like you to do is -- is to try and put the Court in the shoes of an intercept operator working a shift. Typically, what equipment does he have in front of him and what's he doing, typically, in just a few sentences, please?

utterances.speaker: RM316
utterances.text: Very well. In the room there were two desks. On them, we had all of the equipment that was foreseen to monitor and record and reproduce all intercepts. There were two operators in the room. Before them were a number of scanning devices. There was one device assigned exclusively to monitor one channel, then there was a reel-to-reel tape recorder, an UHER, so that would be it, more or less. If you want any other detail, I'll be happy to explain exactly what kind of equipment we had and what each piece was supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. And while an intercept operator is listening to a communication that he has intercepted, how would he know what frequency that particular communication that he's intercepted is on?

utterances.speaker: RM316
utterances.text: The devices had a display where one could see the frequency currently being monitored.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, you mention the reel-to-reel tape recorder which I also understand is known as UHER, and I'd like to discuss the practicalities of the process of using that recorder, that UHER recorder.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, we actually have a physical UHER recorder in the courtroom which, if you think would be of any assistance, we thought we might show to the witness to just basically take us through the mechanics of the recording process. I've discussed this with Mr. Lukic who didn't have any objections. So if Your Honours think it would be of any assistance, then I propose we show it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not entirely clear in what way it would assist us, but the Chamber is willing to take the risk that it will not assist us and nevertheless spend time on it. Always everyone is talking about an UHER recorder, I always understood UHER to be a factory. So therefore not very specific on the type of what we actually look at. But if you would try to do it as efficiently as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'll grab it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- show it to us. Now, the problem, of course, always is that then that becomes a piece of evidence, and should be -- it should be tendered, it should be stored as a --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have a picture of the UHER which is in -- now in evidence as P1561.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. If you think that the actual object adds anything, then that should be in evidence as well. That's the consequence of -- no, if you want to show the picture, then that's no problem. Even markings are more easily made on pictures than on recorders.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: In --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you make experiments, you should think over the legal consequences as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps I'll proceed with my questions with the witness, and if I think it becomes necessary to use the physical UHER, then we can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And use the photograph meanwhile.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Witness, so I'd mentioned I'd like to discuss the practicalities of the recording of an intercept with the UHER machine. Now, in your testimony in the Tolimir case, you state that: "When an intercept operator hears a conversation that he wishes to record, he would press the pause button and the UHER device would start to record." And that's at transcript page 2058. Now, can you please explain this because it sounds strange to say that the recording of a conversation begins once the pause button is pressed? So could you explain that, please?

utterances.speaker: RM316
utterances.text: Yes. At the moment when I spoke those words, I had the image of an UHER in my mind which continues to record when you press the pause button for the second time. And there is another model where when you press the pause button you would stop the recording. That may be the route of the misunderstanding. When you wanted to record a conversation, you would have to release the pause button for the recording to start. You asked me when we would start to record. We would do so at the moment when we heard the beginning of a conversation. We even got a signal when somebody's phone rang, and we were ready to release the pause button which would immediately start the recording. However, if those conversations were very short, we sometimes were unable to record it or catch the beginning because we were busy doing something else, and then the conversation could begin with -- before we were able to release the pause button.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So if I understand your evidence correctly, the UHER machine is already set to record but the pause button is on, thereby preventing recording. And when a conversation begins that the operator wants to record, he released the pause button and the recording begins?

utterances.speaker: RM316
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Now, you mention that there was sometimes -- now, you mention that there were occasions on which you fail to catch the -- the beginning of a recording because you were busy doing something else. Now, again, in a few sentences, can you -- can you explain to the Court why that might be the case? Why there might be a delay between an operator hearing a conversation and the recording of that conversation actually starting?

utterances.speaker: RM316
utterances.text: It did happen. I don't know how often. The operator was a device ready to record on the reception side, but nobody is talking. And then he moves to another device and uses it to scan frequencies to find another potential interesting conversation. It could happen for someone to set up a connection and say, "Hello, this is so-and-so, I need to speak with so-and-so," and then we couldn't react so fast as to release the pause button immediately. But we would then put down on paper that a conversation between X and Y started on channel so-and-so at time stamp so-and-so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you mentioned that you would make a notation on a piece of paper about who the conversation was between and the time that it started. Now, was this piece of paper different to those pieces of paper upon which somebody would transcribe the conversation that was recorded?

utterances.speaker: RM316
utterances.text: Yes. That sheet of paper was separate from the other paper on which that conversation was subsequently reproduced. This former sheet of paper was a small slip on which we noted the conversations, including the elements that are mentioned. Sometimes those conversations were not urgent. It wasn't so important for them to be reproduced immediately. Then we would continue to record other conversations. And when we thought it necessary to reproduce them, we went back to that slip of paper with the elements jotted down on it, and we also read the counter of the device so that the conversation could easier be located on another device. So it was a manner to save time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And just so that I am clear, the transcriber of the conversation, the subsequent transcriber of the conversation, would they have access to this small slip of paper noting down the identities of the individuals involved in the conversation?

utterances.speaker: RM316
utterances.text: Yes. The transcriber would get it together with the tape. And then he would reproduce the conversation using both of these.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could the -- Your Honours, could the Court officer please bring to our screens 65 ter 21028A. And while that's coming up, this is an intercept dated the 16th of July, 1995, between Main Staff duty officer and General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like you to look at the intercept on the screen before you and let me know whether you recognise this as an intercept report prepared by your unit. Please take your time.

utterances.speaker: RM316
utterances.text: Yes. This is our reproduction. We did this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And can you explain how you are able to identify this as originating from your unit?

utterances.speaker: RM316
utterances.text: Every time we would type the heading CSB/SDB Tuzla, the date and the number at which this would be filed, and then the following remarks, on the above date, monitoring, et cetera. So you see the frequency, the channel, the participants, and the time-frame. This is characteristic and this is how we proceeded in all reports, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, the introduction to this intercept indicates that General Mladic was inaudible and in the conversation itself the other participant does not refer to General Mladic by name. Despite this, the person that transcribed this intercept identifies General Mladic as a participant in the conversation. Can you explain how he could have done so?

utterances.speaker: RM316
utterances.text: Let me first say that in no reproduction of ours we stated names unless we had heard them or identified them in a different way. In this case, I suppose that the switchboard operator said, "You have General Mladic on the line," which was not recorded nor was it reproduced, but the operator noted that in the introductory part.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And in the B/C/S version of the intercepts, we see a combination of letters and numbers at the bottom of the intercept report. Can you explain these, please?

utterances.speaker: RM316
utterances.text: Yes. These are the code names or the code designations of the employees of state security. In any correspondence, the employees instead of using their full name they would state this code which consisted of a string of letters and numbers. Those were the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And is there any significance to the order in which these letters and numbers appear?

utterances.speaker: RM316
utterances.text: Yes, I forgot to say that. It was our practice for the one who recorded the conversation is mentioned first, and the second one mentioned is the employee who reproduced the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender that as the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 21028A receives P1655, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1655 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, it just disappeared from our screens but I saw some handwriting. Is that handwriting on the last document translated as well? Perhaps you check that. Well, to have two times the B/C/S doesn't help us in seeing whether it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: It doesn't appear to be translated, Your Honours. I can -- I can request a translation of the handwritten part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please have a look at it. I take it that the Defence is better able to identify what approximately is written there and how relevant and important that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, we could also ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we can ask the witness. Can you read what is written next to the words "very urgent" in handwriting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It says "negotiations about civilians." This is obviously a working version and this was added as a remark that this is about civilians. I don't believe that it bears any deeper meaning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And do you have any idea who could have written that? Or do you either recognise the handwriting, or was there a routine? Who could add handwriting to such reports?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that I may even have been the one who wrote this as a suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What do you mean by "as a suggestion"? For us to understand who wrote that or any other suggestion in any other way? Could you please repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This reproduction is from the northern location, it arrived at the communication centre encrypted over the radio, and it was received at the headquarters of our service. I went to that room very often. When such a document came in, I would read it and write such a remark for the employee who was going to receive this document. I now -- I wrote this to point out that this was about civilians and that's all the significance it has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I do you definitely recognise your handwriting or is it just that you consider it possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is my handwriting, after all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we keep the document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Witness, I see but next to the handwriting there is a "very urgent" writing and it appears in the B/C/S version of the document. Can you explain why there is English there?

utterances.speaker: RM316
utterances.text: Yes. In these communications, depending on the urgency of individual bits of information, in the upper part, where you can read this "very urgent" label, we indicated some such things. Some reports weren't really all that urgent but were still labeled as very urgent.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: But why did you use the English words "very urgent" in this B/C/S communication?

utterances.speaker: RM316
utterances.text: It was a qualification. It was part of the terminology used by our service. We used this very phrase, although it's an English phrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: We can take that document down.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Witness, we've discussed the process of recording of the intercepted communications, and you've referred to pieces of paper on which notations were made at the start of the conversations and which were used to transcribe the communications from the recorded tapes. Now, were these individual pieces of paper or were they part of notebooks?

utterances.speaker: RM316
utterances.text: At that time, we didn't have notebooks. We couldn't procure enough. That is why I procured sheets of paper. I even remember very well how I was able to do so and how I brought them to the location. They were used in a firm for electronic data processing. They were blank sheets and with perforated rims, and we used those. There were also other kinds of paper in use but we mostly used this type.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And as regards the tapes that you used, the tapes used in the UHER recorders, was each intercepted communication recorded onto a separate tape or were the tapes reused?

utterances.speaker: RM316
utterances.text: In practice we would record the conversation on a tape and mark it in the fashion that I've described. If at any point a very urgent or important conversation would begin, we would immediately take it off and -- or, rather, record it and reproduce it. We recorded those on a special tape, on UHER machine, and also mark the counter readings for that specific conversation as well as the exact time and date. That's how we made sure that the tape from which we copied that could be used for further recordings, because we didn't have a sufficient supply of audiotape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I seek some clarification there, especially in view of the terms used. You said: "If at any point a very urgent or important conversation would begin, you would immediately take it off -- or, rather, record it and reproduce it." What do you mean by reproduction, that you would copy it on another tape apart from the tape on which it was initially recorded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is what it was like. There was a reception set, a tape recorder on which we recorded conversations, registered them, I explained to you how we went about it, and then suddenly a very interesting conversation begins. We immediately remove the tape and put it on another recorder for that other person to reproduce it - that is, type it up on paper - then transfer it to a computer, encrypted it, and forwarded it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said you immediately removed the tape. That is, therefore, a tape on which a number of conversations are recorded. You take that tape off, put it on another recorder, and then start working on writing down what then should be the last conversation that was recorded on that tape. Is that how I have to understand it?
